[QUERY] What is your single main symptom or problem right now?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient presents with a year-long history of severe vulvar itching.

[RESPONSE] My main problem right now is severe vulvar itching that I've had for about a year.

[THOUGHT] Chronic vulvar itching has many causes that localize differently; knowing exact distribution (labia majora/minora, perineum, perianal, intravaginal) helps narrow differential (e.g., lichen sclerosus often perianal and labia, candidiasis involves vulva + vaginal discharge, contact dermatitis more labial/groin). I need a single specific location question.

[QUERY] Is the itching confined to the external vulva (and if so which parts: labia majora, labia minora, clitoral hood), or does it also involve the vaginal canal and/or the area around the anus?

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient presents with a year-long history of severe vulvar itching.

[RESPONSE] The itching is vulvar (external vulva) and has been present for about a year. I don't have information in my records about which specific parts of the vulva are affected (labia majora, labia minora, clitoral hood) or whether the vaginal canal or area around the anus are involved.

[THOUGHT] Age and menopausal status strongly influence the differential (lichen sclerosus in older/postmenopausal, chronic dermatitis/lichen simplex in younger). I need the patient's age as a single, specific data point.

[QUERY] How old are you (or what is your age group / menopausal status)?

[REFERENCE] 1. 60-year-old female.
5. Menopause occurred 8 years ago.

[RESPONSE] I'm 60 years old and went through menopause 8 years ago.

[THOUGHT] In a 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with chronic vulvar itching, lichen sclerosus is a leading possibility; key distinguishing sign is white, porcelain-like atrophic patches or scarring. I need to know whether she has visible white/atrophic changes on the vulva to prioritize diagnosis and whether a biopsy is indicated.

[QUERY] Do you notice any white, shiny or thin (porcelain-like) patches, or scarring/skin thinning on your vulva? (Yes/no)

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure; I don't recall noticing any white, shiny, or thin (porcelain-like) patches, or scarring/skin thinning on my vulva.

[THOUGHT] Pain or dyspareunia would suggest an inflammatory or scarring condition (e.g., erosive lichen planus) or other causes requiring urgent exam; absence favors lichen sclerosus/lichen simplex or contact dermatitis. I need one clear symptom data point before requesting an exam.

[QUERY] Do you have vulvar pain or pain with intercourse (dyspareunia)? (Yes/no)

[REFERENCE] 3. The patient presents with a year-long history of pain during sexual intercourse that has gradually worsened.
9. Sexually active with her husband until recently due to severe pain.

[RESPONSE] Yes. I have had pain during intercourse for the past year that has gradually worsened, and I was sexually active with my husband until recently because of the severe pain.

[THOUGHT] In a 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with one year of severe vulvar pruritus and progressive dyspareunia, lichen sclerosus is high on the differential (common in this age group, causes intense itch, atrophic/white patches and scarring leading to dyspareunia). Erosive lichen planus or neoplastic processes are also possible and would present with erosions, ulceration, or suspicious lesions. Visual inspection of the vulva is essential to look for porcelain-white atrophic patches, fissures, erosions, architectural changes (labial fusion), or any suspicious mass; histologic confirmation with a targeted punch biopsy is needed if findings are present or diagnosis is uncertain.

[TEST] Perform a careful vulvar examination (external inspection of labia majora/minora, clitoral hood, perineum and perianal area) with documentation of color (white/erythematous), texture (thinning, erosion, lichenification), fissures, scarring or architectural loss; and obtain a punch biopsy of any abnormal/atrophic/erythematous/erosive lesion(s) for histopathology.

5. External Genitalia: Dry, thin, white plaque-like lesions on the vulva.
6. External Genitalia: Atrophy of the labia minora.
7. External Genitalia: Retraction of the clitoris.
8. External Genitalia: Pale and wrinkled perianal skin.
14. Biopsy of vulvar lesions histopathology: Hyperkeratosis with a thinning of the epidermis and loss of rete ridges, sclerotic changes in the dermis.

[THOUGHT] The combination of a 1-year history of severe vulvar pruritus and progressive dyspareunia in a 60-year-old postmenopausal woman, clinical findings of porcelain-white plaque-like lesions, labial minora atrophy, clitoral retraction and pale perianal skin, plus biopsy showing hyperkeratosis, thinning of the epidermis with loss of rete ridges and dermal sclerosis, is diagnostic. These features are classic for vulvar lichen sclerosus.

[DIAGNOSIS] Vulvar lichen sclerosus.
